title: Hagia Sophia (537)
hook: a dome that seemed to hang from heaven; a later story says Justinian claimed he'd outdone Solomon

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephrem, and your line was the harp of the spirit: theology you could sing. What song got stuck in your head, and what was it teaching? Day eight hundred.

A historian named Procopius walks into a new church in Constantinople and tries to describe the roof. He can't quite manage it. The great dome, he writes, doesn't seem to rest on stone at all. It seems to hang from heaven on a golden chain. And the light, he says, doesn't seem to come in from outside. It seems to be born inside the place. There's a later story, too, that the emperor Justinian walked in on the day it was dedicated and said he had outdone Solomon, who built the temple in Jerusalem. Whether he said it or not, the story stuck. Today's word is the name of that church.

Hagia Sophia is Greek for holy wisdom. The church wasn't named for a saint called Sophia. It was named for the wisdom of God, and Paul, in the King James words, calls Christ "the wisdom of God." The book of Proverbs, in the King James Bible, pictures wisdom as a builder: "Wisdom hath builded her house." Here was a house built in her name. Procopius, who wrote about the emperor's buildings, is our eyewitness. He describes a dome so wide and so light that it seemed to float, and a ring of windows around its base, so the sun pours in just below the curve. That's the trick behind the hanging dome. The light comes in under it, and the solid part seems to lift off. Now the Solomon story. The Bible's Solomon, dedicating his own temple, said something humbler. In the King James words: "But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?" So the builder of the temple in Jerusalem says no house can hold God. Some readers hear that as the honest center of any great church. The dome isn't a container for God. It's a shape that points past itself, an attempt to make stone and light say something about heaven. Hagia Sophia has had a long life since. It has been a cathedral, then a mosque, then a museum, and today it is a mosque again, prayed in by Muslims and visited by people of every faith and none. Orthodox Christians still remember it as the great church of Constantinople. Tomorrow and the days after, we'll come back to this city and what happened inside its churches. Today, just look up.

Here's the practice: look at a photo of the dome. If you have your phone, search for the inside of Hagia Sophia's dome, looking straight up, and let it fill the screen. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes go first to the ring of windows, the light coming in. Then up into the curve. Then to the very top. Don't analyze it. Just let it be big. If you pray, you can let Solomon's question sit with you as you look: will God indeed dwell on the earth? If you don't pray, simply notice what happens in you when you look up for a long time. The bell holds the time.
Hagia Sophia. Holy wisdom: the great church of Constantinople, whose dome seemed to hang from heaven on a ring of light.
Your line: a dome of light. Today, stand under one high ceiling, a station, a library, a tree, and look straight up for a full breath. Day eight hundred.

notes: The title carries the date 537 from the index; the spoken script states no date. Confirm.
Procopius, Buildings 1.1: the dome seems suspended from heaven by a golden chain; light seems generated within; windows around the base of the dome. Paraphrased; confirm.

The Justinian 'I have outdone thee, Solomon' line comes from a later anonymous Narration (Diegesis), not from a contemporary; attributed as 'a later story'. The index hook states it plainly; the script hook line was adjusted. Confirm.
Holy Wisdom identified with Christ (cf. 1 Corinthians 1:24): confirm the wording 'which Christians identified with Christ himself'.
History line 'a cathedral, then a mosque, then a museum, and today a mosque again' is not from the cited texts; it is stated neutrally. Confirm it is current and fair to Muslim and Orthodox readers.
howItsDone: 'many Orthodox churches are built around a central dome, often with an image of Christ' (Pantocrator) is a general claim; confirm or soften.

Editor pass: 'which Christians identified with Christ' now rests on 1 Corinthians 1:24 (KJV, quoted and cited); 'the first great house of God' (superlative) became 'the temple in Jerusalem'; 'the honest center of every great church' softened to 'some readers hear'; 'people have told it ever since' became 'the story stuck'.
